title: Pod Anatomy 101 🧬
description: A deep dive into the Pod – the smallest unit in Kubernetes.

slides.title: What’s Inside a Pod? 🎁
slides.content:
# More than a wrapper

A Pod is a logical host for one or more containers. It provides:
- **Shared network namespace** – all containers share the same IP and port space
- **Shared IPC namespace** – can communicate via System V semaphores or POSIX shared memory
- **Shared storage volumes** – volumes are mounted into all containers
- **Unified lifecycle** – they are scheduled, started, and stopped together

slides.title: Networking Inside a Pod 🌐
slides.content:
## localhost really is local

Containers within a Pod can reach each other on `localhost`. Example:
- Container A listens on `localhost:8080`
- Container B can `curl localhost:8080`

This works because they share the same network stack (including the loopback interface).

**Warning:** Ports cannot overlap. Two containers cannot both bind to port 8080.

quizData.question: Can two containers in the same Pod bind to the same port?

options.text: No, they share the network namespace
Only if they are on different networks

quizData.explanation: They share the same IP and port space, so port conflicts cause failure.

slides.title: The Pause Container ⏸️
slides.content:
## The invisible helper

Every Pod contains a special container called the **pause container** (or sandbox container). It:
- Holds the network namespace for the whole Pod
- Does nothing but sleep
- Ensures the namespace exists even if application containers crash

When you run `docker ps` on a node, you’ll see a `pause` container for every Pod.

slides.title: Why It Matters 💡
slides.content:
## Debugging tip
If you exec into a Pod and can't find a process, remember the pause container is PID 1. The main application containers have their own PID namespace unless you share it.

slides.title: Shared Volumes 📂
slides.content:
## Exchange files easily

A Pod can define volumes that are mounted into all containers. This lets a sidecar container process logs, sync files, or share configuration.

Example: an `emptyDir` volume shared between a web server and a content updater.

```yaml
volumes:
  - name: shared-data
    emptyDir: {}
containers:
  - name: app
    volumeMounts:
      - name: shared-data
        mountPath: /data
  - name: sidecar
    volumeMounts:
      - name: shared-data
        mountPath: /data
```

quizData.question: True or False: Each container in a Pod gets its own copy of the volume.
quizData.explanation: Volumes are shared – all containers see the same data.

slides.title: Full Pod Spec Example
slides.content: A minimal Pod YAML with one container:
slides.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:1.25
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80

quizData.question: What value must 'kind' have to create a Pod?
quizData.explanation: kind: Pod tells Kubernetes to create a Pod resource.
